big_case_rationale: Whether States may demand documentary proof of citizenship on their own registration forms and purge noncitizens inside the 90-day window reaches every State's registration regime, sits at the center of the national election-integrity debate, and follows two emergency-docket interventions; the consent-decree question adds a federalism holding of its own.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority reverses on statutory grounds, not on the consent decree: it holds that proof of citizenship on a state-developed form is information 'necessary to enable' officials to assess eligibility under 52 U.S.C. 20508(b)(1), reading 'necessary' as useful or plainly adapted to a State-defined qualification rather than indispensable, anchored on Inter Tribal Council's line that state forms 'may require information the Federal Form does not' and on avoiding Qualifications Clause doubts; that the 'equivalent' clause of 20506(a)(6)(A)(ii) governs only what public-assistance agencies distribute and cannot support an injunction against the state form itself; and that 'ineligible voters' in 20507(c)(2)(A) means once-eligible registrants, so removing never-eligible noncitizens falls outside the 90-day bar. The LULAC consent decree, resting on consent alone with no adjudicated federal violation, cannot sustain a new injunction against a later statute (Horne v. Flores, Rufo, Frew).

The holding is categorical rather than Arizona-specific: the Court announces that any State may require documentary proof of citizenship on its own mail registration form for federal elections, and that the NVRA's 90-day quiet period never applies to the removal of noncitizens however systematic the program, without confining either rule to Arizona's statutory definition of eligibility (A.R.S. 16-101, 16-121), to the trial record on the operation of H.B. 2243, or to the bifurcated federal-only registration system. The one place the opinion stays narrow is the consent decree: rather than a general rule on when decrees yield to later statutes, it holds only that this decree, resting on consent alone and premised on then-existing state law, cannot ground the injunction below, and leaves modification of the decree itself to a Rule 60(b) motion in the issuing court.
